old:
A DNACPR decision is about CPR only. DNACPR means 'do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation': a decision not to try to restart the heart if it stops.

In UK guidance, every other treatment and all care should still be offered on its merits. A national review of NHS practice found the decision was often treated as if it meant 'do not provide active treatment'.

In a UK scenario study, 231 nurses were randomly given the same deteriorating patient. With a DNACPR form, they planned fewer checks, calls for help and treatments. When the CPR decision sat inside a wider treatment plan, they planned the same care as with no form. This tested intentions, not real care.

If someone you care for has a DNACPR decision, ask the team: what will still be done?

old:
A DNACPR decision is about CPR only. DNACPR means 'do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation': a decision not to try to restart the heart if it stops.

In UK guidance, every other treatment and all care should still be offered on its merits.

That is not always how it is read. A national review of NHS practice found that DNACPR decisions were often treated as if they meant 'do not provide active treatment'. Staff in some studies expected fewer checks, fewer calls for senior help, and changes to pain relief and fluids.

A UK randomised scenario study tested this. 231 nurses were given the same deteriorating patient. Some saw a DNACPR form, some a form that set the CPR decision inside a wider treatment plan, and some no form. The DNACPR group planned fewer checks, fewer calls for help and fewer treatments. The wider-plan group planned the same care as the no-form group. The study measured what nurses said they would do, not real care.

Writing the decision inside a whole plan has also been tried in practice. In one English hospital, a one-page plan replaced the stand-alone DNACPR form. After that, there were fewer harmful events in patients not for CPR. This was a before-and-after study in one hospital, run by the people who developed the plan, so it shows an association, not proof.

The ReSPECT form (Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment) is used across much of the UK. It records the CPR recommendation inside a wider emergency care plan. In English hospitals, about 8 in 10 forms also recorded another treatment recommendation. Most still focused on CPR.

We should write every CPR decision together with a list of what continues. A decision about one treatment says nothing about a person's worth.

If someone you care for has a DNACPR decision, ask: what will still be done?

old:
Staying alive without dementia or lasting disability was the main outcome in a trial of daily aspirin. The trial, ASPREE, gave aspirin or a dummy tablet to 19,114 healthy people aged 70 and over in Australia and the USA.

Lasting disability meant being unable, or finding it very hard, to wash, dress, use the toilet or walk for at least 6 months.

Aspirin did not improve that outcome. Each year, about 21 in every 1000 people in each group died, developed dementia or developed lasting disability. Almost 10 years of follow-up showed the same. Over about 5 years, serious bleeding happened to about 4 in 100 people on aspirin and 3 in 100 on dummy tablets.

This trial was about people who had never had a heart attack or stroke. If you take aspirin after one, keep taking it unless your doctor advises otherwise.

old:
Staying alive without dementia or lasting disability was the main outcome in a trial of daily aspirin. The trial, ASPREE, gave aspirin or a dummy tablet to 19,114 healthy people aged 70 and over in Australia and the USA. The age limit was 65 for US Black and Hispanic participants.

Lasting disability had a concrete meaning: being unable, or finding it very hard, to do a basic daily task for at least 6 months. Examples are washing, dressing, using the toilet and walking.

The results:
1. Aspirin did not improve the main outcome. Each year, about 21 in every 1000 people in each group died, developed dementia or developed lasting disability. Almost 10 years of follow-up showed the same.
2. Heart attacks, strokes and heart failure admissions were not clearly reduced.
3. Over about 5 years, serious bleeding happened to about 4 in 100 people on aspirin and about 3 in 100 on the dummy tablet.

The trial stopped early because continuing was unlikely to show a benefit. In the final year, only about 6 in 10 people in each group were still taking their tablets, which would dilute any effect.

We should expect trials of preventive treatment in older people to report an outcome built on washing, dressing and walking alongside disease events. It tells an older person something a list of heart events alone does not.

One caution applies to every retelling. ASPREE was about people who had never had a heart attack or stroke. For people who have, trials show aspirin prevents further ones. If you take aspirin after a heart attack or stroke, keep taking it unless your doctor advises otherwise.

old:
Some cancer researchers count a one-hour blood test as a whole day. They call these contact days: any day you have to go somewhere for health care.

In six US trials in advanced prostate, lung and pancreatic cancer, people aged 65 and over typically had health care contact on nearly 1 day in 5 in the year after joining.

The count leaves out the family member who drives, waits and sits with you.

Days taken are one side of the decision. In one trial of a drug for advanced bowel cancer (median age 63), people whose tumours had no KRAS mutation (a gene change in the tumour), a group picked out after the trial and the one the drug helps most, had more contact days on the drug (a median of 41 against 10) and more days at home (186 against 132). Across everyone in the trial, days at home did not differ clearly (140 against 121).

Before agreeing to a treatment, you can ask: how many days will this take, and what might it give back?

In six US trials in advanced prostate, lung and pancreatic cancer, people aged 65 and over had health care contact on nearly 1 day in 5 of the time they were followed. That was about the first year after joining.

The count leaves out the family member who drives, waits and sits with you.

Time spent in treatment is only part of the decision. One trial tested a drug for advanced bowel cancer (median age 63). The middle person given the drug had 28 contact days, against 10 given supportive care alone (care to control symptoms, without the drug). Days at home, counted over the rest of their lives, did not differ clearly overall (140 against 121).

One group did differ. People whose tumours had no KRAS mutation (a gene change in the tumour) had more contact days on the drug: the middle person had 41, against 10. They also had more days at home: 186 against 132. This group is the one the drug helps most, and it was picked out after the trial.

Before agreeing to a treatment, you can ask: how many days will this take, and what might I gain from it?

old:
Some cancer researchers count a one-hour blood test as a whole day. They call these contact days: any day a person has to go somewhere for health care. That can be a blood test, a scan, a drip, an emergency visit or a night in hospital.

The numbers are large for older people. In six US trials in advanced prostate, lung and pancreatic cancer, people aged 65 and over had a median of 48 contact days in the year after joining. The typical person spent nearly 1 day in every 5 this way. People were followed for different lengths of time. A study in Mexico of older people having cancer treatment to control, not cure, their disease found a similar share.

The count still leaves things out. It does not include the time family members spend driving, waiting and sitting with the person. The cost of a treatment day is often shared.

Treatment can still be worth the days it takes. In the CO.17 trial, people with advanced bowel cancer were randomly given either weekly drip treatment (cetuximab) or supportive care alone (median age 63). The treated group had a median of 28 contact days, against 10. Among people whose tumours had no KRAS mutation (a gene change in the tumour), the group the drug helps most and one picked out after the trial, treatment took more days (a median of 41 against 10). It also gave more days at home (186 against 132). Across everyone in the trial, days at home did not differ clearly (a median of 140 against 121). Days taken are one side of the decision. Days given back are the other.

Questions you can ask before agreeing to a treatment:
1. How many days a month is this likely to take, counting tests and check-ups?
2. How far will I travel, and who needs to come with me?
3. What is it likely to give back, in time at home or in how I feel?

Clinicians should offer this information when discussing options. Older people can ask for it.
